operationalization: Regress mammalian compositional and phylogenetic similarity (Jaccard/Sorensen and phylobetadiversity) between continental/near-continental islands and their nearest mainland against minimum sea-channel bathymetric depth, controlling for geographic distance and island area.

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species (Spatial Data)
candidate_datasets.role: Global native range polygons and island occurrences for terrestrial mammals

candidate_datasets.name: GEBCO Gridded Bathymetry Data
candidate_datasets.role: Global sea-floor depth grids to compute minimum channel depth (sill depth) between islands and adjacent mainland

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife Mammals Phylogeny
candidate_datasets.role: Time-calibrated mammal trees to quantify phylogenetic divergence of island taxa from mainland relatives

obstacles: Anthropogenic introductions and Holocene extinctions on islands must be filtered out using native/extinct status flags.

Partial regression or generalized dissimilarity modelling separating bathymetric depth (~120 m Pleistocene shelf threshold) from geographic distance is straightforward and directly tests Darwin's claim.

operationalization: For endemic species on oceanic islands globally, identify their sister clades or congeneric species using molecular phylogenies and taxonomy, and test whether the geographic source of nearest relatives is significantly more often the nearest mainland/island source than a more distant region with closer climatic match.

candidate_datasets.name: GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits)
candidate_datasets.role: Regional checklists, endemic status, and floristic affinities for oceanic islands and mainlands worldwide

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: Bioclimatic variables to quantify physical/climatic similarity between oceanic islands and candidate continental regions

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Synthetic phylogenetic trees to identify sister taxa of island endemics across plants and animals

obstacles: Incomplete species-level phylogenetic sampling for hyper-diverse island invertebrate groups.
Stepping-stone dispersal along now-submerged seamounts or paleocurrent pathways can make the 'nearest' source differ from straight-line geographic distance.
rationale: Global island floras and vertebrate faunas are well catalogued alongside gridded climate data and synthetic phylogenies. Comparing phylogenetic/taxonomic affinity against geographic proximity versus climatic similarity across oceanic archipelagos provides a direct, quantitative test.

operationalization: For endemic species across multiple islands within oceanic archipelagos, compute the proportion whose nearest phylogenetic relative (sister species or clade) occurs on another island of the same archipelago rather than outside the archipelago.

candidate_datasets.name: GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits)
candidate_datasets.role: Island-level endemic species lists across oceanic archipelagos

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic relationships among archipelago endemics and continental relatives

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Sequence data underlying clade-level phylogeographic studies of island radiations (e.g. Hawaii, Galapagos, Macaronesia, Canary Islands)

obstacles: Multiple independent colonizations of an archipelago from the mainland can produce congeners on different islands that are each closer to a mainland ancestor than to one another.
High rates of anthropogenic extinction on islands (especially birds and land snails) remove sister species.
rationale: Archipelago-level checklists and phylogenetic trees for vascular plants, birds, reptiles, and many insects are publicly accessible. Testing whether intra-archipelago sister relationships predominate over extra-archipelago relationships is a standard phylogeographic analysis doable within weeks.

operationalization: Calculate the proportion of naturalized alien species belonging to genera absent from the recipient native flora/fauna, and compare the mean nearest-taxon phylogenetic distance (MNTD) between naturalized species and native assemblages against null draws from the global donor pool (Darwin's naturalization hypothesis).

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF (Global Naturalized Alien Flora)
candidate_datasets.role: Global occurrences and taxonomic identities of naturalized alien vascular plant species across regions

candidate_datasets.name: GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits)
candidate_datasets.role: Native regional floras to determine presence/absence of native congeners and phylogenetic distances

candidate_datasets.name: GRIIS (Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species)
candidate_datasets.role: Country- and island-level checklists of introduced and naturalized plants and animals

obstacles: Human introduction bias (propagule pressure and deliberate selection of novel crop/ornamental genera) confounds natural establishment filters.
Spatial scale dependence: phylogenetic repulsion at local neighborhood scales can coexist with phylogenetic attraction (environmental filtering) at regional scales.
rationale: Known in modern ecology as Darwin's Naturalization Hypothesis, this claim has been extensively operationalized and tested using GloNAF, GIFT, and GRIIS. All required taxonomic and phylogenetic data are openly downloadable and can be analyzed rapidly.

operationalization: Across discrete habitat islands (oceanic islands, sky-island mountains, ancient lakes, and cave systems), test whether endemic species have their sister taxa in the nearest accessible source region/surface habitat and exhibit divergent functional traits correlated with local habitat regimes.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility)
candidate_datasets.role: Georeferenced species occurrences across insular, montane, freshwater, and subterranean habitats

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic placement of insular, alpine, lacustrine, and troglobitic endemics relative to regional source lineages

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Functional trait measurements to evaluate divergence of island and alpine plants from lowland source relatives

obstacles: 'Better fitted to their new homes' requires demonstrating local adaptation (reciprocal transplants or fitness assays), which cannot be inferred purely from trait divergence in observational databases.
Cave and marsh biotas have much sparser global phylogenetic and trait coverage than oceanic islands and alpine zones.
rationale: The biogeographic and phylogenetic component—that inhabitants of islands, mountains, lakes, and caves are most closely related to species from the nearest accessible source region—is readily testable with existing occurrence and phylogenetic databases. However, proving that their modifications make them 'better fitted' requires fitness data not available across the broad scope.

operationalization: Across pairs of non-adjacent biogeographic regions or floristic/faunistic provinces, test whether pairs sharing a high number of sister species or congeneric endemics ('representative species') also share at least some identical native species and elevated proportions of subspecies/infraspecific taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: WCVP (World Checklist of Vascular Plants)
candidate_datasets.role: Global distributions of vascular plant species, subspecies, varieties, and synonymy across TDWG botanical countries

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility)
candidate_datasets.role: Global species and subspecies occurrence records across animals and plants

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic hierarchy, infraspecific ranks, and synonymy counts as a proxy for 'doubtful forms'

obstacles: Taxonomic philosophy (splitting vs. lumping across regional floras and faunas) directly affects whether populations in two regions are scored as identical species, subspecies, or distinct representative species.
Ancient vicariance (e.g. Gondwanan or Eastern Asian–Eastern North American disjunctions) can leave shared genera/sister clades after all identical species have diverged.
rationale: Regional checklists with species, infraspecific taxa, and taxonomic synonymy counts exist globally (e.g., WCVP across TDWG regions). Testing the correlation between shared congeners/sister species, shared identical species, and infraspecific/synonymy rates across region pairs is fast and directly evaluates Darwin's universal prediction.

operationalization: Operationalize 'position in the scale of nature' via standard proxies corresponding to Darwin's examples (non-vascular vs. vascular plants, unicellular/invertebrate vs. vertebrate animals, or cell-type count), and test whether species geographic range size correlates negatively with organismal complexity and propagule size.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility)
candidate_datasets.role: Global georeferenced occurrences to estimate geographic range extent across major plant, animal, and microbial clades

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Seed and spore mass data across bryophytes, ferns, gymnosperms, and angiosperms

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxon duration and evolutionary turnover rates across higher taxa to test the 'change more slowly' mechanism

obstacles: 'Lower' versus 'higher' in the scale of nature is not a modern biological concept and requires proxy definitions (e.g. traditional taxonomic rank order or cell-type number).
Cryptic speciation discovered via molecular barcoding frequently reveals that supposedly cosmopolitan 'lower' morphospecies are complexes of narrow-range species.
Sampling effort in global occurrence databases is heavily skewed toward vertebrates and flowering plants compared with microscopic or 'lower' taxa.
rationale: While Darwin's notion of a 'scale of nature' requires translating into the specific taxonomic contrasts he discusses (e.g. cryptogams vs. flowering plants, invertebrates/microbes vs. vertebrates) or propagule size, global range-size, trait, and fossil-duration datasets exist to test both the range-size pattern and the proposed mechanisms.

operationalization: Using independent molecular phylogenies and fossil-calibrated trees, correlate patristic phylogenetic distance between pairs of species within a class against their geographic distance (centroid/minimum range distance) and temporal distance (stratigraphic gap between fossil occurrences).

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Pairwise divergence times and molecular phylogenetic distances across thousands of living species

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility)
candidate_datasets.role: Geographic distributions of extant taxa to calculate pairwise spatial distances

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic age ranges and paleocoordinates of fossil taxa to measure temporal and spatial proximity

obstacles: If trees are constructed using stratigraphic or biogeographic priors, testing temporal/spatial proximity becomes circular; strictly sequence-based or morphology-only trees must be used.
Long-distance dispersal and sympatric/allopatric speciation dynamics create high variance at very shallow phylogenetic scales.
rationale: With independent molecular phylogenies (built solely from sequence data), testing whether closer genealogical relatives are on average closer in geographic space and stratigraphic age is non-circular and feasible across major classes using TimeTree, GBIF, and PBDB.

operationalization: Compare morphological disparity matrices of extant clades against the same clades including extinct stem/intermediate fossils, testing whether hierarchical clustering structure (cophenetic correlation and gap statistics) becomes significantly more nested and discrete when extinct intermediates are removed.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Published morphological character matrices containing both extant and extinct fossil taxa across major clades

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic hierarchies and extinction records of fossil lineages

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Hierarchical taxonomic structure of extant organisms

obstacles: Any purely branching birth-death process automatically produces a tree topology, so separating selective extermination of intermediates from neutral stochastic extinction requires testing whether morphologically intermediate lineages go extinct at higher rates.
Fossil morphological matrices cover only skeletal/hard-part characters for a subset of clades.
rationale: We can empirically test with existing paleontological character matrices (MorphoBank) whether adding extinct taxa fills morphological gaps and reduces the discreteness of nested clusters among extant taxa. However, testing the full mechanistic claim across all life and distinguishing selective competition from random branching extinction is only partially achievable.

operationalization: Test whether pre-molecular (morphology-based) Linnaean classifications predict independent neutral molecular phylogenies (e.g. synonymous substitutions or non-coding genomic trees) far better than chance and better than purely ecological/functional groupings.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Taxonomy
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic classifications alongside independent genomic sequence data

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Comparison of traditional taxonomic hierarchies with molecular phylogenetic trees

obstacles: The claim that propinquity of descent is 'the only known cause' of similarity is partly conceptual/explanatory and contrasts with non-empirical creationist ('plan of creation') alternatives.
Modern classifications have largely been revised using phylogenetic data, so historical pre-molecular classifications must be used to avoid circularity.
rationale: Although framed as a conceptual explanation of what naturalists meant by the 'Natural System', the empirical core—that natural classifications reflect genealogical descent rather than mere adaptive resemblance—can be tested non-circularly by comparing classical morphological classifications against neutral molecular phylogenies.

operationalization: Across published morphological character matrices mapped onto independent molecular phylogenies, measure each character's phylogenetic signal (consistency index / retention index) and test whether characters tied directly to foraging/locomotory ecology show lower consistency and less diagnostic utility at higher taxonomic ranks than non-ecological characters.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Annotated morphological character matrices across animal and plant clades

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Independent molecular reference trees onto which morphological characters can be mapped

obstacles: Classifying morphological characters a priori into 'concerned with special habits' versus 'little changed in adapting species' requires manual annotation and can be subjective.
Systematists historically pre-selected conserved characters when building morphological matrices, biasing available datasets.
rationale: MorphoBank contains thousands of coded morphological characters that can be mapped onto independent molecular trees to compute evolutionary lability and homoplasy (Consistency and Retention Indices). Partitioning characters by ecological function tests Darwin's prediction, though functional categorization of traits requires moderate curation.

operationalization: Test whether clades assigned to the same Linnaean rank (e.g. genus, family, order) exhibit huge, overlapping variance in crown age, molecular divergence, and phenotypic disparity across the tree of life, and whether rank elevation historically correlates with species richness rather than standardized divergence.

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Crown and stem divergence ages for thousands of genera, families, and orders across eukaryotes

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic rank assignments and species richness per higher taxon

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Taxonomy
candidate_datasets.role: Lineage rank classifications paired with sequence divergence data

obstacles: Part of the claim is conceptual (that taxonomic rank has no intrinsic ontological metric), though its empirical manifestations—lack of consistent divergence thresholds and sensitivity to species discovery—are directly measurable.
rationale: Comparative studies of TimeTree and Catalogue of Life readily quantify the massive overlap in divergence ages and genetic distances among genera, families, and orders across and within classes, directly testing and confirming that Linnaean ranks lack uniform quantitative thresholds.

operationalization: For sister clades in time-calibrated molecular phylogenies (which by definition share identical time since divergence from a common progenitor), test whether sister branches frequently differ substantially in accumulated morphological disparity, evolutionary rate, and assigned Linnaean rank.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Sister-clade topologies paired with traditional Linnaean rank assignments

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological character matrices to measure asymmetric phenotypic branch lengths between sister lineages

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Time-calibrated phylogenies verifying equal temporal age of sister lineages

obstacles: Post-cladistic taxonomy increasingly eliminates paraphyletic groups and equalizes sister-group ranks, so pre-cladistic or rank-asymmetric classifications must be examined to test the second part of the claim.
rationale: Sister clades share the exact same genealogical proximity to their common ancestor. Measuring phenotypic branch-length asymmetry on MorphoBank matrices and comparing assigned taxonomic ranks across sister lineages is a clean, quantitative test achievable with existing public data.

operationalization: Using genome-wide SNP and morphological datasets of domestic breeds (e.g. dogs, cattle, pigeons, crops) and wild subspecies, test for significant hierarchical tree-like structure (treelikeness / delta-score / cophenetic correlation) matching historical breed genealogy and unequal branch lengths.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA)
candidate_datasets.role: Population genomic datasets of domestic breeds (dogs, horses, pigeons, livestock) and wild varieties

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Published SNP genotype and morphometric matrices of domestic dog, pigeon, and crop breeds

obstacles: Reticulate evolution (intentional cross-breeding and introgression among domestic varieties) introduces admixture edges that partially violate a strictly nested tree.
rationale: Genomic and morphometric datasets for dozens of domestic species (including Darwin's own model, domestic pigeons and dogs) and wild subspecies are publicly available. Testing whether varieties form nested genealogical clusters with varying branch lengths is a standard phylogenetic and population-genetic analysis.

operationalization: Map non-adaptive or rudimentary morphological characters shared across ecologically diverse species onto independent molecular phylogenies, and test whether they show significantly higher phylogenetic consistency (synapomorphy retention) and clade recovery power than ecologically adaptive characters.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological character matrices containing vestigial/rudimentary and minor structural characters across clades

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Independent molecular reference phylogenies to evaluate clade monophyly predicted by shared characters

obstacles: Secondary loss or independent reduction of rudimentary structures across sub-lineages can create homoplasy among rudiments.

rationale: Using independent molecular phylogenies as ground truth for common inheritance, we can directly test whether minor and rudimentary characters shared across species with contrasting ecological habits accurately diagnose monophyletic clades.

operationalization: Across distantly related clades occupying the same ecological guild (e.g. fossorial, aquatic, gliding, myrmecophagous mammals, or succulent plants), test whether external ecomorphological traits cluster by ecological regime (high homoplasy between groups) rather than molecular phylogeny, while still tracking phylogeny within a single shallow clade.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Global morphological trait and ecological guild dataset for all birds to test ecomorphological convergence vs. phylogeny

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Phenotypic character matrices across vertebrate and invertebrate clades

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife Mammals Phylogeny
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular phylogenies to contrast true genealogical affinity with ecomorphological clustering

obstacles: Separating 'external adaptive characters' from deeper anatomical characters requires trait-category annotations.
rationale: Convergent ecomorphological evolution across distant lineages occupying similar niches—and the failure of such traits to recover deep phylogeny while remaining informative within shallow clades—can be rigorously quantified today using global trait databases (like AVONET or mammal trait compilations) paired with molecular trees.

operationalization: Using the fossil record, test whether clade richness in time bin t positively predicts net diversification and expansion in bin t+1 while negatively predicting survival of ecologically overlapping smaller clades, and compare the resulting taxonomic hierarchy against neutral birth-death (Yule/coalescent) expectations.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global fossil occurrences through the Phanerozoic to track clade richness trajectories, dominance replacement, and extinction

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Distribution of species richness across higher taxonomic ranks (hollow-curve distributions)

obstacles: Neutral stochastic branching (Yule process) with random extinction also produces a hollow-curve distribution where all extant species trace back to a few surviving deep lineages, making it hard to discriminate competitive supplanting from neutral drift without explicit clade-competition models.
Mass extinctions periodically reset incumbency and overturn dominant groups regardless of gradual competitive superiority.
rationale: Paleobiology Database records allow testing whether speciose clades preferentially expand and whether their rise correlates with the decline of smaller ecological competitors. However, because neutral birth-death processes also generate hollow-curve hierarchies where few deep clades survive, discriminating power is moderate.

operationalization: Identify phylogenetically isolated, species-poor extant clades ('aberrant groups' with high Evolutionary Distinctiveness, e.g. Monotremata, Sphenodontia, Dipnoi, Ginkgoales) and test in the fossil record whether their stem/crown groups formerly had much higher taxonomic diversity and elevated cumulative extinction rates, and whether surviving species have long internal divergence times.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil richness and extinction histories of clades that are today species-poor and phylogenetically isolated

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Stem and crown divergence ages demonstrating deep isolation and high inter-specific divergence among surviving relict species

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Tree topologies and sister-group sizes across living clades

obstacles: Fossil preservation bias against small, soft-bodied, or tropical forest taxa means some phylogenetically isolated extant groups lack a fossil record to verify past diversity.

rationale: For groups with a fossil record (vertebrates, molluscs, arthropods, vascular plants), PBDB and TimeTree directly test whether today's phylogenetically isolated, species-poor clades had higher past diversity that suffered heavy extinction, and whether their few extant species are separated by deep divergence times.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Multi-order morphological character matrices to compare character-state sharing with ancestral reconstructions vs. terminal species

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Reference phylogenies defining sister-group and outgroup relationships

obstacles: Convergent adaptation to a specialized niche shared with a particular species in another group can occasionally produce special (apomorphic) rather than general (plesiomorphic) resemblance.

operationalization: Quantify morphological disparity and nearest-neighbor morphospace gaps between extant vertebrate classes (e.g. Aves vs. Reptilia, Mammalia vs. Reptilia, Tetrapoda vs. fishes) before and after including extinct stem-group fossils (e.g. non-avian theropods, non-mammalian synapsids, stem tetrapods), testing whether fossils systematically bridge the inter-class morphospace intervals.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Cladistic character matrices spanning major class transitions (theropod-bird, synapsid-mammal, fin-to-limb)

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stratigraphic occurrences and taxonomic distributions of extinct stem-group vertebrates

obstacles: Soft-tissue, physiological, and behavioral characters separating extant classes rarely fossilize, restricting the test to skeletal morphology.

operationalization: Represent anatomical structures within a class (e.g. tetrapod limb skeletons, vertebrate skulls, arthropod appendages) as anatomical connectivity graphs where nodes are homologous elements and edges are articulations, and test whether topological adjacency order is conserved across species despite orders-of-magnitude variation in element dimensions.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon (Uber-anatomy Ontology)
candidate_datasets.role: Formal ontology encoding homology, partonomy, and topological connectivity relations of anatomical structures across animals

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D CT scans and mesh datasets of vertebrate skeletons across classes to measure shape/size variation vs. topological connectivity

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative anatomical character matrices across vertebrate and arthropod classes

operationalization: Perform ancestral character state reconstruction of homologous organ patterns (e.g. pentadactyl tetrapod limb, generalized insect mouthparts) on time-calibrated phylogenies incorporating stem fossils, testing whether a single ancestral node possessed the shared topological groundplan and whether descendant trajectories trace continuous step-wise modifications correlated with ecological function.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological character matrices for tetrapod limbs, mammal skeletons, and insect mouthparts including fossil taxa

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences and temporal sequence of early stem and crown group members

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life

operationalization: Using Cambrian/Paleozoic fossil character matrices and comparative phylogenetics of vertebrates, panarthropods/annelids, and angiosperms, test whether stem progenitors possessed homonomous (serially repeated, weakly differentiated) segments/appendages/floral whorls compared with derived crown groups that show increased serial differentiation (tagmosis/heteronomy).

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological matrices of Cambrian panarthropods, early vertebrates, and basal angiosperms coding serial appendage/floral differentiation

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database

rationale: Published paleontological and evo-devo datasets (including Cambrian arthropod matrices in MorphoBank and the eFlower dataset for angiosperms) directly test whether ancestral progenitors had more uniform, repeated serial elements that subsequently differentiated—and also allow refuting specific sub-claims like the vertebral origin of the entire skull.

candidate_datasets.name: Bgee (Gene Expression Evolution Database)

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO)
candidate_datasets.role: Cross-species developmental time-series RNA-seq datasets testing the developmental hourglass/funnel model

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon (Uber-anatomy Ontology)

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Independent molecular phylogenies confirming clade placement of sessile and parasitic taxa (e.g. Cirripedia within Pancrustacea, Tunicata within Chordata)

candidate_datasets.name: Bgee (Gene Expression Evolution Database)
candidate_datasets.role: Developmental gene expression profiles across embryonic and adult stages

obstacles: Secondary loss of larval stages (direct development) or convergent larval adaptations (e.g. planktotrophic larval convergence) can occasionally confound larval-only trees.
rationale: Using independent molecular phylogenies as the benchmark for true community of descent, we can quantitatively compare the phylogenetic accuracy (retention index, Robinson-Foulds distance to genomic trees) of embryonic/larval characters versus adult characters in MorphoBank matrices, directly confirming Darwin's claim.

operationalization: For clades with rich fossil stem series and well-characterized ontogenies (e.g. mammals/synapsids, birds/theropods, echinoderms, trilobites), test whether early embryonic/juvenile skeletal character states of extant species match adult character states of basal stem fossils significantly more often than extant adult states do.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Cladistic matrices coding ontogenetic transformations alongside stem-group fossils (e.g. middle ear ossicles in synapsids, wrist/pelvic bones in dinosaur-bird transition)

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D developmental series of extant vertebrate skeletons and CT scans of stem fossils

obstacles: As Darwin himself noted in the claim, the geological record lacks the earliest soft-bodied progenitors of most phyla and classes.

Embryonic soft-tissue stages do not fossilize, limiting direct comparison to biomineralized late-embryonic/perinatal structures (e.g. Meckel's cartilage and ear ossicles, avian tarsometatarsus/carpometacarpus fusion, ammonoid/trilobite protoconchs).
rationale: While deep soft-bodied embryos cannot be compared to Precambrian ancestors, late embryonic ossification sequences in living vertebrates (e.g., mammalian jaw-to-ear ossicle development, avian digital and tarsal fusion) and juvenile shells/exoskeletons in invertebrates can be quantitatively compared with adult stem fossils using MorphoBank and MorphoSource.

operationalization: Test across developmental time-series datasets whether evolutionary divergence in morphology and gene expression (and the phylostratigraphic age or dN/dS of expressed genes) is lowest at early/mid-embryonic stages and increases progressively toward late development and adulthood.

candidate_datasets.name: Bgee (Gene Expression Evolution Database)
candidate_datasets.role: Stage-annotated multi-species transcriptomic data to quantify evolutionary divergence across developmental time

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO)
candidate_datasets.role: Developmental time-course RNA-seq datasets across vertebrate, insect, and nematode clades

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl Compara
candidate_datasets.role: Orthology, sequence divergence (dN/dS), and gene age across metazoan genomes to pair with stage-specific expression

obstacles: Modern evo-devo data show a 'developmental hourglass' (highest conservation at the mid-embryonic phylotypic period, with higher divergence in both earliest cleavage and late post-organogenesis stages) rather than monotonic conservation from zygote onward, which directly tests and partially refines Darwin's early-vs-late model.
rationale: Translated into modern developmental genetics and comparative embryology, Darwin's model ('late-appearing variations inherited at corresponding ages') predicts increasing interspecific divergence and relaxed selective constraint from organogenesis to adulthood. Public developmental transcriptomes (Bgee, GEO) paired with comparative genomics (Ensembl) test this directly across multiple phyla.

operationalization: Query large comparative morphological matrices and anatomical ontologies across major plant and animal clades for the prevalence of reduced, vestigial, or non-functional character states (e.g. staminodes, pelvic vestiges, reduced wings/eyes, pseudogenes).

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological character matrices coding reduced, vestigial, or rudimentary character states across thousands of animal and plant taxa

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon (Uber-anatomy Ontology)
candidate_datasets.role: Cross-species anatomical ontology documenting vestigial and rudimentary structures

obstacles: 'Extremely common' has no strict quantitative threshold, and proving 'uselessness' (complete lack of secondary function) for an anatomical structure is notoriously difficult without experimental ablation.
Systematists do not uniformly label reduced character states as 'vestigial' or 'rudimentary' across all matrices.
rationale: While 'extremely common' and 'bearing the stamp of uselessness' have qualitative boundaries, morphological character matrices in MorphoBank and anatomical ontologies document thousands of unambiguous rudimentary structures (staminodes in flowers, vestigial limbs in squamates/cetaceans, reduced wings in flightless insects/birds), allowing a broad quantitative survey across clades.

operationalization: Compare the intraspecific coefficient of variation (CV) and interspecific evolutionary rate of rudimentary/vestigial structures against functional homologous structures in the same individuals or sister clades (and analogously compare dN/dS or polymorphism in pseudogenes/dispensable trait loci vs. functional loci).

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D skeletal scans allowing intraspecific and interspecific measurement of vestigial vs. functional elements (e.g. pelvic rudiments, reduced digits, vestigial teeth)

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Published morphometric datasets comparing phenotypic variance of vestigial vs. functional traits across individuals and species

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Polymorphic character state scoring in rudimentary vs. functional characters across closely allied species

obstacles: Measurement error inflates the coefficient of variation (CV) for very small structures unless carefully controlled for size scaling (e.g. using Taylor's power law residuals).
Some rudimentary structures acquire secondary functions (e.g. cetacean pelvic bones in reproductive musculature) and remain under stabilizing selection.
rationale: Comparing intraspecific phenotypic variance (CV, controlling for mean size) and interspecific divergence between vestigial traits and functional traits within the same organisms is a clean, quantitative test directly executable with morphometric datasets in Dryad, MorphoSource, and MorphoBank.

operationalization: Measure the relative size (allometric ratio of rudiment dimension to body size or adjacent functional element) of rudimentary organs in embryonic/fetal stages versus adult stages across taxa (e.g. baleen whale tooth buds, ruminant upper incisors, kiwi/ostrich wing skeletons, limb-reduced squamate limb buds) and test whether the embryonic ratio universally exceeds the adult ratio.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D micro-CT and diceCT scans of embryonic and adult specimens of cetaceans, flightless birds, and limb-reduced reptiles

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Ontogenetic character matrices documenting transient embryonic structures (e.g. tooth primordia in mysticetes and edentulous vertebrates)

obstacles: As a 'universal rule', a single well-documented exception (an organ arrested before primordium formation) would technically falsify strict universality, though across macroscopic rudiments negative allometry after embryogenesis is widely measurable.
Embryonic 3D scan series in public repositories cover dozens of model and non-model vertebrates, but fewer plants and invertebrates.
rationale: Relative size of a rudiment in embryo versus adult is a straightforward morphometric ratio (negative ontogenetic allometry). High-resolution diceCT and micro-CT embryonic and adult scans on MorphoSource and ontogenetic data in MorphoBank allow direct quantitative verification across Darwin's exact examples and beyond.

operationalization: In cave animals and flightless island birds, use molecular evolutionary analyses (dN/dS, RELAX selection tests, and QTL/GWAS of eye and wing reduction) to test whether trait regression is driven primarily by neutral mutation accumulation under relaxed selection ('disuse' in modern genetic terms) versus positive directional selection (energy economy / pleiotropy).

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative genomic sequences of cavefishes (e.g. Astyanax mexicanus), subterranean mammals, and flightless island birds

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: Annotated genomes including Astyanax mexicanus (cavefish) and flightless/flighted paleognath and rail birds

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Published molecular evolution and QTL datasets testing relaxed vs. positive selection in eye and wing reduction

obstacles: Darwin's literal mechanism of 'inherited effects of disuse' (Lamarckian somatic disuse transmitted to offspring) is refuted by modern genetics; testing the claim requires either refuting the literal Lamarckian inheritance mechanism or reinterpreting 'disuse' as relaxed purifying selection versus positive selection.

Distinguishing relaxed purifying selection from positive selection on regulatory enhancers requires dense population-genomic and functional data available only for well-studied systems like Astyanax mexicanus and paleognaths.
rationale: Literal Lamarckian inheritance of somatic disuse can be refuted using existing genetics datasets, while the modernized question—whether organ regression in cavefish and island birds stems mainly from relaxed selection (non-use) versus direct positive selection—is actively tested using public comparative genomes (Ensembl, GenBank, Dryad). The need to reinterpret 'disuse' lowers operationalizability.

operationalization: Test for statistically significant common ancestry (tree-like phylogenetic signal via Whitehouse/Penny congruence tests, shared endogenous retroviruses/transposon insertions, and sequence likelihood ratio tests against independent origins) across all orders within each classical animal and plant class.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Orthologous protein and nucleotide sequences across all orders within every animal and plant class

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Comprehensive phylogenetic synthesis demonstrating monophyly or shared descent of members within classes

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological and paleontological matrices linking orders within classes

obstacles: Some 19th-century classes (e.g. 'Radiata', 'Pisces', 'Reptilia' excluding birds) were paraphyletic or polyphyletic, though all their members still share common descent within a slightly broader clade.
rationale: Common descent of all members within each class is overwhelmingly testable and resolvable using formal statistical tests of common ancestry (tree congruence across independent loci, shared rare genomic changes, and fossil intermediates) on publicly available genomic and morphological databases.

operationalization: Test using universal core orthologous genes and rare genomic changes across all extant animal phyla (Metazoa) and land plant/green plant divisions (Viridiplantae/Archaeplastida) whether animals trace back to <= 5 ancestors (in fact 1, monophyletic Metazoa) and plants to <= 5 ancestors (1, monophyletic Plantae).

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: Proteome-wide orthologous protein sequences across all animal phyla and plant divisions

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Genomic and transcriptomic sequences across all metazoan and plant clades

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Global phylogenies testing monophyly of Metazoa and Archaeplastida/Embryophyta

obstacles: 19th-century definitions of 'plants' sometimes included fungi and diverse algae acquired via secondary endosymbiosis, which would increase the count of eukaryotic photosynthetic lineages to a few independent endosymbiotic events—still consistent with 'at most four or five'.
rationale: Darwin framed this cautiously ('at most four or five progenitors'), making it an upper-bound hypothesis. Phylogenomic analysis of publicly available proteomes and genomes across all animal phyla and plant divisions cleanly tests and confirms that Metazoa and Embryophyta/Archaeplastida each descend from a single common progenitor (well within <= 4–5).

operationalization: Quantify the conservation of core biochemical pathways (ATP, nucleic acids, universal genetic code, ribosomal translation, central carbon metabolism), cellular lipid-membrane architecture, and cross-kingdom toxin target conservation across Archaea, Bacteria, Plantae, and Animalia.

candidate_datasets.name: KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes)
candidate_datasets.role: Universal metabolic and cellular pathway maps across thousands of bacterial, archaeal, plant, and animal genomes

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: Universal protein families and conserved biochemical machinery across all domains of life

candidate_datasets.name: ChEMBL
candidate_datasets.role: Bioactivity data for small molecules and toxins across orthologous targets in plants, animals, fungi, and microbes

obstacles: While universal biochemical and cellular features are directly quantifiable, phrases like 'laws of growth and reproduction' are broad umbrella terms.
rationale: Public pathway and proteome databases (KEGG, UniProt) and bioactivity repositories (ChEMBL) provide exhaustive, quantitative evidence across thousands of sequenced organisms showing shared macromolecular composition, cellular structure, core metabolic networks, and conserved target sensitivity to poisons.

operationalization: Apply formal statistical tests of Universal Common Ancestry (UCA, e.g. Theobald's likelihood ratio / AIC test and tree-congruence tests across universally conserved translational/transcriptional proteins and optimality of the universal genetic code) comparing a single primordial origin (LUCA) against multiple independent origins of Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya.

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: Universally conserved orthologous protein sequences (ribosomal proteins, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, RNA/DNA polymerases) across all domains of life

candidate_datasets.name: GTDB (Genome Taxonomy Database)
candidate_datasets.role: Standardized bacterial and archaeal phylogenomic alignments and trees

candidate_datasets.name: PDB (Protein Data Bank)
candidate_datasets.role: 3D structural folds of universally conserved informational proteins across Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya

obstacles: Extinct pre-LUCA stem lineages that left no surviving descendants cannot be directly sampled, though UCA of all known cellular life is directly testable.
Extensive horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in early cellular evolution requires modeling reticulation alongside vertical descent.
rationale: Darwin's famous inference of a single primordial form (Universal Common Ancestry / LUCA) has been directly operationalized and tested in modern bioinformatics (e.g. Theobald 2010 and subsequent structural/sequence tests) using public sequence and structure databases (UniProt, GTDB, PDB).

operationalization: Test whether pairs of recognized varieties/subspecies and closely related species lie along a continuous gradient of genetic divergence (Fst, dXY) and reproductive isolation (The 'speciation continuum' / grey zone of speciation) with extant gene flow/hybrid zones in varieties and extinct/historical coalescence in species.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA)
candidate_datasets.role: Population genomic datasets across the 'grey zone' of speciation (0.5% to 2% net synonymous divergence) in animals and plants

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative datasets of reproductive isolation vs. genetic distance and speciation-continuum meta-analyses

obstacles: Whether species are 'combinations made for convenience' versus real biological units defined by intrinsic reproductive isolation (Biological Species Concept) is partly a conceptual/definitional debate.
Instantaneous speciation (e.g. allopolyploid speciation in plants) can produce reproductive isolation in a single generation without a protracted series of intermediate gradations.
rationale: The empirical assertion—that varieties and species form a continuous gradation where varieties remain connected by extant intermediates/gene flow while species were connected in the past—is testable using speciation-continuum population genomic datasets. However, the prescriptive taxonomic claim ('combinations made for convenience') is conceptual, making the overall claim partially resolvable.

operationalization: In time-resolved fossil records and dated phylogenies, compare the relative variance in origination, extinction, and phenotypic evolution rates explained by biotic interactions (diversity-dependent clade competition, predator-prey escalation) versus abiotic environmental forcing (paleotemperature, sea level, bolide/volcanic perturbations)—the Red Queen vs. Court Jester hypothesis.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global Phanerozoic fossil occurrences to model biotic diversity-dependence vs. abiotic turnover across clades

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) Paleoclimatology
candidate_datasets.role: Paleoclimate proxy time series (d18O, d13C, sea level, temperature) to test abiotic forcing of evolutionary change

obstacles: Biotic and abiotic drivers operate simultaneously and interact (and vary by temporal/spatial scale: Red Queen at local/short scales vs. Court Jester at global/macroevolutionary scales), making a single universal dominance ranking hard to isolate cleanly.
Direct organism-to-organism ecological interactions are rarely preserved in the fossil record and must be inferred from co-occurrence and functional guild proxies.
rationale: In macroevolution, this claim corresponds directly to the classic 'Red Queen vs. Court Jester' debate. Public fossil occurrence data (PBDB) paired with paleoclimate proxy time series allow fitting birth-death and phenotypic evolution models comparing biotic versus abiotic predictors, though scale-dependence and indirect interaction proxies limit discriminating power.

operationalization: Correlate taxonomic turnover (proportion of species/genera replaced or Bray-Curtis/Forbes dissimilarity) and morphological divergence between consecutive geological formations/stages against independent radiometric age differences (Ma) across the Phanerozoic.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stage- and formation-level fossil assemblages across the Phanerozoic to compute faunal/floral turnover between consecutive formations

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Chronostratigraphic gap durations, formation boundaries, and absolute radiometric age models for geological units

obstacles: Episodic mass extinctions and rapid environmental shifts cause pulsed turnover that deviates from a strictly constant 'paleontological clock', testing Darwin's qualifier that it is a 'fair, though imperfect, measure'.
rationale: Darwin had no radiometric dating in 1859, so this was a bold forward prediction. Today, independent radiometric dates (U-Pb, Ar-Ar) integrated in Macrostrat and the International Chronostratigraphic Chart can be correlated directly against faunal turnover between consecutive formations in PBDB, cleanly testing how well organic change measures elapsed time.

operationalization: Compare taxonomic origination/turnover rates and morphological/genomic diversification rates across major geological eras—specifically Archean/Proterozoic microfossil and biomarker records versus early Paleozoic and late Phanerozoic records.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Proterozoic and Phanerozoic fossil occurrences to calculate cohort longevity and taxonomic turnover rates over geological time

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Deep time-calibrated molecular trees spanning Archean, Proterozoic, and Phanerozoic divergences

obstacles: The Archean and early Proterozoic fossil record consists mostly of morphologically conserved microbial mats and acritarchs, where morphological stasis may mask biochemical/metabolic evolution.

Even within the Phanerozoic, taxonomic turnover rates decline rather than accelerate from the Cambrian/Ordovician toward the Recent, whereas Precambrian acritarch/stromatolite turnover was genuinely much slower than Phanerozoic metazoan turnover.
rationale: Cohort survivorship and turnover analyses using PBDB and Precambrian microfossil compilations (showing very long taxon durations in the Proterozoic 'Boring Billion' compared to the Phanerozoic, alongside changing rates within the Phanerozoic) directly test Darwin's hypothesis, though preservation limits resolution at 'the first dawn of life'.

operationalization: Compute the ratio of the duration of the classical fossil-bearing geological column known in 1859 (Cambrian to Recent, ~539 Myr) to the total radiometrically dated duration since the earliest paleontological/isotopic evidence of life and molecular clock estimates of LUCA (~3.8–4.2 Gyr).

candidate_datasets.name: International Chronostratigraphic Chart (ICS)
candidate_datasets.role: Official radiometrically calibrated ages of the Phanerozoic (Cambrian base 538.8 Ma) and Precambrian eons (Archean/Hadean to 4,567 Ma)

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular clock divergence estimates for LUCA and early Precambrian divergences (>3.8–4.0 Ga)

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Radiometric age compilation of Precambrian and Phanerozoic rock units

obstacles: If 'history of the world as at present known [in 1859]' means the Cambrian-to-Recent fossiliferous column, it is indeed ~13% of life's history; if reinterpreted as modern radiometric knowledge of Earth's crust, it spans most of life's history.
rationale: In 1859, the known fossiliferous geological record began at the base of the 'Silurian' (now Cambrian, ~539 Ma). Radiometric dating (ICS, Macrostrat) and molecular clocks (TimeTree) establish that life originated ~3.8–4.2 Ga, meaning the post-Cambrian geological history known to Darwin was indeed only ~13% (a small fragment) of the time elapsed since the first organism.

operationalization: Map standardized cognitive benchmark scores (inhibitory control, spatial memory, numerical competence, social cognition) and neuroanatomical correlates (encephalization quotient, pallial/neocortical neuron counts) across vertebrate phylogenies to test for phylogenetic signal and continuous evolutionary gradation.

candidate_datasets.name: ManyPrimates / Comparative Cognition Datasets (via OSF)
candidate_datasets.role: Open standardized comparative cognition datasets across primates, birds, and carnivores

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative neuroanatomical datasets (brain size, neuron counts, endocast volumes) and behavioral trait compilations across vertebrates

obstacles: Cognitive capacities do not fossilize directly, so evolutionary gradation must be inferred from comparative phylogenetic reconstructions across extant species and fossil endocast volumes.
Testing 'each mental power' comprehensively is limited by the difficulty of designing species-fair cognitive tasks across distantly related taxa.
rationale: While programmatic statements about the future foundation of psychology are not directly empirical, the core biological claim—that cognitive capacities and their neural substrates vary by continuous gradations with strong phylogenetic continuity across animals—can be partially tested today using comparative cognition datasets (e.g. ManyPrimates on OSF) and neuroanatomical databases on Dryad.

operationalization: Treat historical geological time bins in the fossil record as retrospective 'presents' and test whether: (1) only a small fraction of species in bin t leave descendant lineages surviving to bin t + k, and (2) species with wide geographic occupancy, high abundance (occurrence frequency), and membership in speciose higher taxa have significantly higher long-term survival and descendant diversification.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global time-binned fossil occurrences to measure geographic range size, occurrence frequency, clade richness, and long-term lineage survival/diversification

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Abundance and range dynamics of Cenozoic/Quaternary taxa across time intervals

obstacles: Wide geographic range and high abundance also increase fossil sampling probability, so capture-mark-recapture (CMR / PyRate) models must be used to separate true survival and speciation from preservation bias.
Mass extinction events (e.g. K-Pg) sometimes eliminate dominant, speciose clades despite wide species ranges, altering background selectivity rules.
rationale: Although stated as a prophecy about living species, the law is directly testable retrospectively across dozens of time intervals in the Paleobiology Database. Using occupancy, occurrence frequency, and clade size in time bin t to predict lineage persistence and descendant richness in subsequent intervals is a standard paleobiological analysis.

operationalization: Test in the global fossil record whether any stratigraphic boundary (including the Big Five mass extinctions) shows 100% lineage extinction (zero boundary-crossing clades/lineages), and test whether molecular time-trees of extant organisms show continuous coalescent lineages extending pre-Silurian (>443 Ma) without a post-Silurian total reset.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Global stratigraphic range-through data across all Phanerozoic stage boundaries showing survival of boundary-crossing lineages even through major mass extinctions

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Time-calibrated phylogenies showing hundreds of extant lineages diverging before the Silurian (>443 Ma) and persisting continuously to the present

obstacles: If 'cataclysm has desolated the whole world' is read strictly as total global sterilization (Cuvierian/d'Orbigny global annihilation and re-creation), it is decisively refuted; if read loosely as global severe mass extinctions (e.g. End-Permian, K-Pg Chicxulub impact) that devastated ecosystems without breaking generational continuity, the fossil record shows global cataclysms did occur while generational continuity was never broken.
rationale: Darwin is explicitly refuting Cuvier/d'Orbigny catastrophism (world-wide cataclysms that wiped out all life and required new creations). Both the Paleobiology Database (range-through survival across every Phanerozoic boundary) and TimeTree (continuous unbroken lineages from pre-Silurian times to today) resolve this claim unambiguously.

operationalization: No non-arbitrary, environment-independent metric of organismal 'perfection' exists across all bodily and mental endowments; any proxy such as local relative fitness is constantly reset by environmental change and coevolution (Red Queen dynamics) rather than progressing monotonically toward an absolute optimum.
obstacles: 'Perfection' of all bodily and mental endowments is a value-laden, teleological concept without an objective, context-free biological metric.
Relative fitness is local to a transient environment, and vestigialization/parasitic simplification routinely reduces anatomical and neural complexity when favored by selection.
rationale: Unlike specific biomechanical efficiencies or short-term experimental evolution fitness gains, a universal tendency of 'all corporeal and mental endowments to progress towards perfection' across all life has no objective, context-independent empirical definition that can be confirmed or refuted by datasets.

operationalization: Decompose the grand synthesis into its component empirical propositions: (1) test whether variation is caused mainly by external conditions and use/disuse (refuted by modern mutation/heritability datasets), (2) test whether reproductive capacity exceeds carrying capacity and drives natural selection in wild populations, and (3) test whether selection drives character divergence and lineage extinction.

candidate_datasets.name: COMADRE and COMPADRE Matrix Databases
candidate_datasets.role: Global demographic matrix population models across thousands of plant and animal species to quantify intrinsic rates of increase

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad Digital Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Meta-analytic datasets of phenotypic selection gradients in the wild (e.g. Kingsolver et al.) and spontaneous mutation rates

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil record of clade divergence and extinction over macroevolutionary time

obstacles: As the book's overarching synthesis ('the entangled bank'), it bundles half a dozen distinct laws into a single macro-claim rather than a single testable relationship.

One bundled component—that heritable variability is generated by the direct/indirect action of external conditions and by use and disuse—is refuted by modern genetics, while the demographic, selective, and macroevolutionary components are supported.
rationale: Because this final sentence synthesizes the entire book's causal chain into one overarching statement, it cannot be resolved by a single unified statistical test. However, its individual empirical pillars (high intrinsic rates of increase in COMPADRE/COMADRE, measurable selection gradients in the wild, and the falsity of use/disuse as the source of heritable variation) can each be tested with existing public datasets.
